s07.slug: SATURDAY · 5:10 PM · DELGADO HALL, THE MAILBOXES
body: The lobby at ten past five smells like the basement laundry has been coming up the elevator shaft all afternoon, sweet and chemical. Marcus is at the front desk behind a yellow highlighter and the organic chemistry book, and he has highlighted so much of the open page that it has gone back to meaning nothing. Jack’s hair is still wet from the fourth-floor shower, and there’s sand in the cuffs of his jeans he’ll be finding till Tuesday. Box 412: a Sigma Rho car-wash flyer, a credit-card offer that calls Theodore A. Vance a valued customer, and an envelope addressed in pencil, block capitals, pressed so hard the letters stand up on the back. In the corner, smaller, the same hand:

body.title: Envelope, top left corner
body.text:
DANIEL F. COSTIGAN
A555218
TRUMBULL CORRECTIONAL INSTITUTION
LEAVITTSBURG, OHIO 44430

body: He doesn’t open it in the lobby. He takes the east stairs instead of the elevator, two at a time to four, where the concrete repeats every footstep half a second late, and sits on the top step of the landing under the window that opens six inches. The Lagoon in the slot. One bar on the RAZR. Nobody. He opens the envelope with his thumb.

body.title: Lined paper, pencil, both sides
body.text:
Professor —
Your ocean letter got here Tuesday. Sixty-six degrees, green on top and gray underneath. I read it to Reggie twice. Reggie’s from Portsmouth, he’s seen the Ohio River, he says same thing. Reggie wants to know does the Pacific smell. Find out and report back, that’s an order.
Brideshead is still in the mailroom. I think a C.O. is reading it. Good for him honestly.
I called the house tonight and Gina picked up and said everything’s fine. Everything’s fine, Danny. She’s been saying fine since she was four years old, that’s how I know it ain’t. You know what it is. Don’t tell me. Tell Gina it ain’t hers to carry. I got it.
Tell the veil girl thanks for asking my name. Nobody out there asks it anymore. They ask Ma how I’m doing like I’m the weather.
Send the Hopkins. Ma says it’s poems. Send it anyway.
Ma says you sound skinny on the phone. Eat something.
—D.

body: So that’s what it was. Thursday on the bluff bench the recorded woman came in over his brother at *tell Gina —* and took the rest of the sentence back to Leavittsburg with her, and the rest of the sentence was already in the mail, in pencil, written the night before anybody had to cut it off.

Out through the six inches of open window the Lagoon is going pewter. Something small and dark — a coot, a grebe; he’s from Youngstown, it’s a duck — draws a line across the water that closes up behind it. Jack keeps his thumb on the fold until the line is gone. Then he folds the letter along Danny’s creases and puts it in his back pocket, flat against Hale’s Williams.

At twenty to six he wedges the RAZR into the top corner of the window frame, where the bar lives, and calls home. Twenty to nine on Glenwood Avenue. His mother picks up on the second ring, the dishwasher going behind her. “Did you eat? Don’t lie, I can hear it.” “Two hot dogs. A priest grilled them.” “A priest,” she repeats, impressed and suspicious at once. Nonna told Father Bruno about the rectory Mass, she reports, in the vestibule after the eight o’clock, where the Iannuccis could hear; Father Bruno says tell him good. Ohio State won. “Your father yelled at the TV, Jackie. In a good way.” Then, in a different voice: “It’s the nineteenth. She lit the candle for Nonno this morning.”
Jack knows what the nineteenth is. Nineteen seventy-seven, a Monday: Sheet & Tube shut the Campbell Works, and Nonno came home before ten with his lunch still in the pail.

A click, the extension in the front room, and the post-game show comes in behind it, two men in sport coats laughing. “Thirty-eight nothing,” his father says. “In Cleveland. You see that?” “I saw it.” He didn’t; he was at a church barbecue with a sprinkler. His father breathes into the phone. “Good. Don’t waste it.” Click.
Then a scuffle at the kitchen end, a chair leg, his mother saying *Regina*, and Gina has the phone. “is the nun’s name a secret —” And his mother has it back. “Nonna wants you.”
The extension in Nonna’s room, three tries, EWTN behind her and a rosary in progress. “Giacomino.” Thin and fierce as a wire. “E la ragazza? The nun?”

So he tells her. The nun painted a fleur-de-lis on his face for the football, and he wore it to Communion by accident. The nun’s team hasn’t lost. The nun said hi to Danny on the telephone, and Danny laughed. Nonna laughs at all of it, the old laugh with the cough on the end, and at the last one she stops and says, “She talk to Danny,” not asking. Then: “Brava. Brava la monaca.”

Then Rosie, thirty seconds, breathless, about the drawing she mailed Tuesday: it’s him at the beach, the orange part is the sun and the other orange part is a crab, and he has to put it on his wall *today*. He promises. Then his mother again — the Iannuccis’ new dog, which is the size of a loaf of bread and hates Frank — and a rustle on the line, and the extension lifting in Nonna’s room. Three tries. The rosary going behind her.
“Giacomino.” The same voice. The same words. “E la ragazza? The nun?”
She’s asking it new. On the kitchen end, his mother has gone quiet.

journal.title: Danny
journal.text: My brother. Trumbull Correctional. Calls me Professor. Ma brought him the good socks. *Brideshead* went to him through Driftwood, margins erased; a C.O. is reading it first. The ocean letter got there; he read it to Reggie, from Portsmouth, who wants to know if the Pacific smells. Lena knows. She asked his name. On the bluff bench she said hi to him and told him she’s going to be defense, and he laughed like he used to. The system cut him off at ‘tell Gina — .’ He wrote the rest down Wednesday night: tell Gina it ain’t hers to carry. He’s got it. Thanked the veil girl for asking his name.

choices.text: Answer her again. The same, like it’s the first time.
choices.key: When Nonna asked about the girl a second time, you answered her like it was the first.
response: So he tells it again. The fleur-de-lis, the Communion line, the team that hasn’t lost, Danny laughing — the same jokes in the same order, with the same pauses where she laughed the first time. She laughs in the same places. At the end she says, “Brava. Brava la monaca,” exactly as before, and he says, “I’ll tell her, Nonna,” as if he hadn’t said it five minutes ago.
Then the rustle, and his mother’s voice, close: “She’s tired, honey.”

A pause with EWTN in it. “So I ask again,” Nonna says. “I’m old, I’m allowed.” She says it fondly, the way she says everything to him, and he can hear in it that she has no idea why he said what he said. Then she wants to know about the girl.
Then the rustle, and his mother’s voice, close: “She’s tired, honey.”
He says it gently. It doesn’t take any doing; his mother is already reaching for the phone, he can hear her crossing the kitchen. “She’s tired, honey.”

s07b.slug: SATURDAY · 6:02 PM · DELGADO HALL, EAST STAIRWELL, 4TH-FLOOR LANDING
body: He stays on the landing after. The RAZR is warm from his ear and the window frame is cold under his hand, and two floors down somebody has the Black Eyed Peas going behind a door, the song the whole building has been playing for a month, the bass coming up the stairwell a step at a time. He’s due at the Anchor at seven. The Lagoon has gone dark at the edges.
At 6:02 the phone goes again.

body: Saturday at the Anchor runs on a different engine from Tuesday. By midnight every booth is Las Olas kids sobering up on hash browns, the Hobart slams its hood every ninety seconds, and the steam has made a weather system of the dish pit that Jack lives inside with his sleeves shoved past the elbow. Somebody in booth six has found the jukebox’s one Mariah Carey and paid to hear it three times.

PIE OF THE DAY, says the chalkboard: KEY LIME. Gloria stops at the pass with the coffee pot and looks back out at booth four, where a boy and a girl in matching Sigma Rho sweatshirts are sharing one slice with two forks and not looking at each other. “Key lime,” she tells Jack, about them. “Looks like a good time, and it’ll make your face do that.” She does the face. It is exactly the face. Then she’s through the door again with the pot.

Rudy has the transistor off tonight — Saturday is too loud for Vin Scully — and a Louis L’Amour in his apron with the spine taped. At ten to twelve, flipping eggs for a table of surfers, he says without turning around, “You wrote him?” “He wrote back.” Rudy nods at the flattop as though the eggs had told him something good. He slides two of them, over easy, onto a plate with rye toast, cut on the diagonal, and sets it on the steel by the Hobart. “Dish man eats.”

At 12:40 the bell over the door, and Rafi Ochoa, skateboard under one arm and a backpack on both shoulders, his hair stiff with salt. He takes a stool at the counter, orders the key lime, and counts exact change onto the Formica. When Jack comes out with a rack of clean mugs, Rafi lifts his fork. “Boss.” His family’s place is two blocks up the hill from the wharf; his abuela’s asleep, and what she doesn’t know about pie can’t hurt her. He looks at the clock over the register. “You off at one? I’ll skate you out as far as Las Olas. I got deliveries on Seacliff.”
At 1:12, mopping under the Hobart, Jack feels the RAZR go off in his apron pocket.

body.text: Are you off at one? I’m on the Pi Lam steps. Laney’s staying. I’m sober and I’m the only one. —L.

response: He hangs the apron on the hook by the walk-in. Out on the wharf Rafi is already on the board, rolling slow circles under the sodium light with one hand out for La Flaca’s basket.

choices.text: Text back: is this a rescue
response: Capital letter, period, initial. He hangs up the apron.

He folds the phone and hangs up the apron and has La Flaca off the wharf rail before Gloria can rate his exit. Rafi drops the board, catches the wire basket with one hand going by, and they’re moving.

body: La Flaca has no light. She came to him in August with a basket and a bell and a chain and no light, and for three weeks Jack has ridden Ocean Road home at one in the morning by the white line and memory. Tonight Rafi is behind him on the skateboard with one hand on the wire basket, getting towed, his wheels ticking over every seam in the asphalt. The fog is down to the road. Past the turnoff for St. Brendan’s the Grove starts on the right, the eucalyptus creaking in it and letting go of long strips of bark onto the shoulder.

Headlights come up behind them, slow, and stay slow. Then a light starts turning on the inside of a windshield, red and blue in the fog, and a gray Crown Victoria with no markings and a long antenna eases up level with La Flaca’s back wheel and keeps pace.

The driver’s window comes down. A man in a navy windbreaker leans an elbow out — fifties, by the face; gray in the mustache; a gold badge clipped to his belt that the dome light finds. He holds a badge wallet out the window, open, at reading distance. “Ray Ochoa. Marisol Police.” He gives Jack time to read it. “License and registration.”
To a bicycle.

Jack stops La Flaca on the coaster brake and puts a foot down. Then, because something has to be done and nothing else occurs to him, he works his wallet out of his back pocket from behind the Williams and Danny’s letter and hands over his Ohio driver’s license. The man takes it. He holds it up into the dome light and reads it like the Gospel. “John Anthony Costigan,” he says. “Youngstown.”
“Pop,” says Rafi, coasting up into the light on the board.

The man doesn’t look at his son. He’s still looking at the license. “I know that board from a quarter mile back, Rafael. I paid for that board.” He’s on call, it turns out, westbound, a car break-in on Del Playa. “It’ll keep. That car’s been getting broken into since 1987.” Then something to Rafi in Spanish, fast and low, of which Jack catches *la luz* and *tu abuela* and nothing else, and Rafi answers in Spanish with both palms up.

Ray turns back. “California Vehicle Code, twenty-one two-oh-one, subsection d. A bicycle operated during darkness shall be equipped with a lamp emitting a white light visible from a distance of three hundred feet in front.” More or less; he recites it flat, in one breath. He looks at La Flaca, at the rust and the basket and the bell. “This bicycle was reported abandoned at the harbor in 2007.”
“Not stolen,” Rafi says. “Abandoned. Abuela says there’s a week’s difference.”
“Your abuela is not a court.” Ray hands the license back through the window, and on the way he takes a better look at Jack’s face. “You’re Gloria’s dish man. Rudy’s kitchen.”
And Jack has him, then: Tuesdays, the far end of the counter, meatloaf and black coffee, a man who nods to Rudy through the pass and never says a word to him.

response: “Detective,” Ray says. It comes out warm, almost pleased, and for the first time something in the tired face moves — the mustache, mostly. Rafi, behind Jack, makes a small noise of professional admiration.

choices.text: “It’s his bike. I don’t have a light. That’s on me.”
choices.key: Stopped by Rafi’s father on Ocean Road, you owned the missing light.
response: Ray looks at him through the window with the dome light on both of them, and keeps looking, until Jack starts to wonder if there’s a form. “Huh,” Ray says finally. It’s respect; Jack can hear that much. Rafi looks at Jack as if he’s done something illegal and beautiful.

choices.text: “Is this about the light or the bike?”
response: “It’s about your mouth, Mr. Costigan,” Ray says, without heat, as though it were subsection e. Behind Jack, Rafi is delighted and says absolutely nothing, which is its own kind of noise.

choices.text: Hands on the bars. Say nothing.
response: Jack keeps his hands on the bars where they can be seen and his mouth shut. Ray considers this. Then, to Rafi, in English: “See that? He knows how to get pulled over. You could learn.”

body: Ray looks past him, at Rafi, at the backpack on Rafi’s shoulders. “What’s in the bag, Rafael?”
“Vitamins, Pop.”
Ray looks at his son. It goes on long enough for the dash light to come around four or five times on the side of Rafi’s face, red, blue, red. Then he looks away from the bag.

He puts the car in park and gets out, a hand on the door frame for his knees, and walks back to the trunk, and comes back with a clip-on bike light still on its cardboard. “Found property,” he says. “It’s been found.” He bends over La Flaca’s handlebar and clips it on himself, tests the clamp, and clicks it on, and a cone of white light goes out ahead of them into the fog and gives them twenty feet of Ocean Road they didn’t have before.

Back at the car he leans on the roof and looks at Jack. “He selling you anything?” “No, sir.” It’s the truth. Ray nods. Then he looks off down Ocean Road toward the Grove, toward the dark where the road bends, at neither of them. “I’ve picked enough kids up off this road.”

He gets in. The dash light goes off. The Crown Vic pulls ahead, unhurried, toward Del Playa and the car that’s been getting broken into since 1987, and its taillights go small and red in the fog, and then there’s only the fog.

They roll again. Rafi on the board with one hand on the basket, the new light swinging a little on the bars and laying a white path down for them to ride on. After a hundred yards: “Thanks, boss.” And then, though Jack hasn’t asked and wasn’t going to — Rafi is straight about anything that costs money, whatever it is — “Weed. Adderall around midterms. Not bars, though. I don’t do bars anymore.”

journal.title: Rafi Ochoa (204)
journal.text: Rafi Ochoa. Second floor. Carried my fridge up four flights and was gone before Dad could tip him. Calls everybody boss. Lent me his bike till Christmas. His father’s a detective. He sells weed, and Adderall around midterms. Not bars, he says.

journal.title: Ray Ochoa (Marisol PD)
journal.text: Detective Sergeant. Rafi’s father. Gray Crown Vic, a windbreaker, the Vehicle Code by heart. Knows my face from the Anchor counter. Did the bit: ‘License and registration.’ Asked what was in the bag and took ‘vitamins’ for an answer. Gave me a light out of his trunk. Found property.

response: “Yeah,” Rafi says. He rides a while on that, the board humming. “He’s a good one. That’s the problem.”
At the top of Seacliff he lets go of the basket with a little push and peels off west toward the surf rentals and his deliveries. The new light carries Jack the last two blocks to Pi Lam alone.
Rafi grins at the fog. “My abuela says the devil’s patient, so be faster.”
At the top of Seacliff he lets go of the basket with a little push and peels off west toward the surf rentals and his deliveries. The new light carries Jack the last two blocks to Pi Lam alone.
Jack rides. A block goes by under the light, then most of another. “Appreciate you, boss,” Rafi says.
At the top of Seacliff he lets go of the basket with a little push and peels off west toward the surf rentals and his deliveries. The new light carries Jack the last two blocks to Pi Lam alone.

body: He makes it down Mission on La Flaca in twenty minutes with Ray’s light still clipped to the bars, burning uselessly at noon. Sully’s smells of Bloody Mary mix and fryer oil. The Saints are on the big screen in white. Third quarter.

Lena is in the booth under it in her Keds, which means she’s happy, holding a coffee the size of a vase in both palms, on what she announces is three hours of sleep. Kevin is across from her in a 49ers cap with a basket of fries arranged by length. “I drove,” he says. “Designated adult. Also designated alarm clock. She answered the door in one shoe.” “I answered the door,” Lena says, “in a state of grace.”

body.text: She slides over to make room for him and says, “Mr. Costigan,” pleasantly, and for the first quarter-hour she is a degree too polite with him — offering him fries, asking after his sleep, passing the ketchup by its base. Then the bell wins.

body: At the end of the bar, Dale Wisniewski in the Barry Sanders jersey turns on his stool, sees Jack, and lifts his coffee an inch. “The loud one.” Last week Dale left a column of quarters and *next week, kid*. It’s next week. Jack lifts a hand back.

The Eagles have a kid at quarterback, first start, because McNabb’s ribs are cracked, and the kid is throwing it all over Philadelphia and throwing it, every so often, to the Saints. Midway through, the Eagles’ return man fumbles a kickoff, and two plays later the Saints are in the end zone, and the owner is on the brass bell with his whole shoulder, and Lena is standing on the booth seat with her coffee held out level so as not to lose any. “The kid’s going to be good,” Dale says of the Eagles quarterback. “You said that about the Lions kid,” Jack says. “I say it about all of them,” says Dale. “One of them’s going to be.”

body.text: At a commercial she leans across the table, very serious. “How are your jeans, Costigan?” “Hanging out the window of 412.” “Like a flag.” “Theo thinks it’s a surrender.” She returns to her coffee, satisfied, and Kevin looks from one of them to the other and eats a fry with enormous discretion.
body.else: At a commercial she props her chin on her fist and looks at him across the fries. “I found half the beach in my bed this morning, Costigan.” “Which half?” “The half with the egrets in it.” She returns to her coffee, satisfied, and Kevin looks from one of them to the other and eats a fry with enormous discretion.

body: At 12:30 the RAZR goes in his pocket.

body.text: Eid Mubarak to the Catholics. I can eat lunch. I’m going to eat it twice.

body: In the fourth the Saints are far enough ahead that Lena has started being gracious about Philadelphia, and then Brees fumbles the ball out of his own end zone for a safety, and she takes it personally. She sits down. She tells Kevin she has been betrayed before God and the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania. Reggie Bush answers for it a few minutes later, nineteen yards untouched, and she stands back up and forgives everybody.

Final, forty-eight to twenty-two. Dale raps the table going out and leaves quarters. In the lot Lena wipes 1–0 off the Odyssey’s back glass with the hem of her cardigan, digs the La Vang car-wash polish out of her tote, and writes it big: 2–0. Kevin, keys out: “Still my mom’s car.” Lena caps the bottle and pats the glass like a horse. “Your mother’s car,” she says, “is undefeated.”

s12b.slug: SUNDAY · 12:15 PM · ISLAMIC CENTER OF MARISOL, MISSION STREET
body: KESSLER SHOES is still ghosted in gold over the door, but under it the storefront has put on its Eid best: paper garlands in green and gold looped across the window, a hand-lettered EID MUBARAK taped to the glass, and inside, the wire shoe racks overflowing onto the sidewalk — men’s loafers, a pair of patent-leather Mary Janes, small sneakers that light up when a kid runs past them, which is constantly. Jack unlaces his boots. He checked his socks before he left Delgado. No holes. Yusuf, at the door, glances down at them anyway. “Progress,” he says.

He’s in a new kurta, pale gray with white thread at the collar, mailed from Fremont by his mother in a box that also contained, he reports, three pounds of dates and a letter about his hair. The folding tables along the back wall are buried: rice in foil pans, kebabs, bolani, a bowl of chickpeas the size of a birdbath, and a steel pot of sheer khurma, vermicelli in sweet milk with cardamom and dates and slivered pistachio, which a grandmother ladles into a paper cup and puts into Jack’s hands without asking his name. Kids in new clothes do laps between the tables. The uncle in the Raiders cap is here, in a better Raiders cap.
“Thirty days,” Yusuf says, loading a plate. “I can eat lunch.” He adds a second kebab. “I’m going to eat it twice.”

At twenty to one his phone goes, and his whole face changes before he’s even got it to his ear. He takes it out onto the sidewalk among the shoes. Through the window Jack watches him walk up and down past the laundromat in his socks, one hand flat on his head. He comes back in five minutes later, lighter by about a hundred pounds. “Tariq,” he says. “It’s ten past midnight there. It’s tomorrow.” He sits down. “He complained about the food. He’s fine.”

Over the second lunch, he explains zakat al-fitr, because Jack asks what the coffee can by the door with the slot in the lid is for. Before the Eid prayer, every household pays for food for the poor — so much per head, babies included. “You pay the poorest man’s breakfast before you’re allowed to pray for yours,” Yusuf says. “So nobody is hungry on the day.” He tears a piece of bolani in half and hands Jack the bigger piece, which Jack is beginning to understand is not an accident. “Load-bearing. You take it out, the feast falls down.”
At 1:16 the RAZR goes.

body.text: 2–0. I slept through the first quarter on Dale’s shoulder. Tell no one. —L.

body: Jack shows Yusuf, because he can’t not. Yusuf reads it and hands the phone back and returns to his chickpeas. “Who’s Dale?” “A Lions fan.” Yusuf nods, as if this explains a great deal about the Catholic Church.

s13.slug: SUNDAY · 9:00 PM · ST. BRENDAN’S, THE COLLEGE MASS
body: At ten to nine the courtyard is full of people in hoodies and the broken sprinkler under the olive tree is hissing at nobody. In the lot beyond the hedge, under the one lamp, the Odyssey’s back glass says 2–0 in big careful pink.

body.text: It’s the first he’s seen of it. She wrote the dash with a flourish.

body: Kevin is at the church door in the navy quarter-zip, handing out worship aids like a maître d’. “Browns lost, man,” he says, by way of hello. “Twenty-seven six.” He gives Jack a worship aid and a consoling squeeze of the shoulder, and Jack takes both.

The college Mass is standing room again: candles, the overheads off, the blue glass black, the hull of the ceiling going up into the dark over everybody. Three guitars and the cajón. Kenzie Rourke cantors the psalm — *The Lord upholds my life* — and her voice goes up into the ribs of the boat and hangs. Then Joey Abruzzo gets up to lector for the first time in his life and reads Wisdom at a volume that would carry across the Staten Island Ferry in a gale. *Let us see whether his words be true.* In the second pew Kevin sits forward with his elbows on his knees, and his lips are moving along with every word; Joey’s been coached. Then James, and one line out of it Jack hears and keeps: *You covet but do not possess.*
Then Mark. The road through Galilee, and the Twelve behind Him, arguing.

Osei preaches from the step with the reading glasses on their cord. “On the road they argued about who was the greatest,” he says. “In the house He asked them what they had been talking about, and they were silent.” He looks out at them over the glasses. “Every one of us has been silent in that house.” And he sits.

Laney is between them. She came in at 8:58 hungover and pink, in her new Pi Lam letters under Lena’s oatmeal cardigan, sunglasses pushed up into the copper hair, and sat down in the middle without discussing it, and now she sits through the Eucharistic Prayer with her eyes shut and her hands folded like she’s seen it done. At the Our Father she takes Lena’s hand and squeezes it, and doesn’t let go of it after the Amen.

At the sign of peace she turns to Lena first. “I’m sorry I called you a mother.” Lena looks at her, at the sunglasses and the letters and the cardigan, which is hers. “Cher,” she says. “Somebody has to be.” Then Laney turns and shakes Jack’s hand with both of hers and great dignity, and over the top of her head Lena gives him her hand, too.

body.text: It’s brief and dry, a hand at Mass. Neither of them mentions the temperature.

body: At Communion Laney goes up between them with her arms crossed over the Pi Lam letters for the blessing, the way she did at her first, like a Baptist, and comes back with her eyes down and her mouth closed tight on something that isn’t a joke.

During the recessional Becca Lindell turns around, two rows up across the aisle — she did it at the peace, too — and waves at him with her whole hand, the whole arm going, a rancher’s wave across a pasture.

journal.title: Laney Price
journal.text: Laney Price. Pi Lam, as of Thursday: ran back across Seacliff in a pink cowboy hat to Lena first. The night before, on the floor of 217 in a white dress, she asked what happens if they look at her and see. First Catholic Mass: arms crossed like a Baptist, came back from the blessing pink and quiet. Programmed herself into my phone. (Hoodie status: hers.) Pi Lam’s barn party: carried upstairs by her new sisters, glorious and wrecked. Called Lena a mother over the banister. Said sorry at the sign of peace, at her second Mass.

journal.title: Kevin Tran
journal.text: Kevin Tran. Goes to daily Mass, saves you a seat with a Bible. Has a sister, Tina, in dental school, who flossed in the womb. Lies to his mom about orgo in Vietnamese. Drives his mother’s Odyssey at sixty-five, not sixty-six. His dad has two nail-salon supply stores in San Jose and has never had a Labor Day. Shadowed in an ER this summer. Tells his mother he’s asleep. Brought six pairs of gloves to a beach cleanup. Coached Joey through his first reading and mouthed every word of it from the second pew.

response: He lifts a hand and waves back, a real wave, and Becca beams like he’s answered something. She points at him over the heads of the people filing out and mouths a word across the aisle. It’s probably *Friday*. The question mark is still on her face when the crowd takes her out the door.
Beside him Lena is very busy finding the sleeve of her own cardigan on Laney.

choices.text: Tell Laney she did beautifully, in Lena’s bulletin voice.
response: He leans down to her ear and gives it the full parish bulletin, the voice of a note written on the back of one: “You are doing beautifully.” Laney goes pink to the hairline. “Sugar,” she says, “I *know*.”
On her other side, Lena keeps her eyes on the recessional and pretends she didn’t hear a word of it. The corner of her mouth gives her away.

He stays down on the kneeler while the church empties around him, hoodies and backpacks, the candles guttering in the draft from the doors. The last guitar chord rings in the hull and quits. He prays the way he always has, short and plain, to Someone in the next room: *Nonna. Danny. Gina. Her. Me, if there’s any left over.*
When he gets up and goes out, Lena and Laney are under the olive tree in the dark, Laney’s head on Lena’s shoulder, waiting for him.

s13b.music: The Avett Brothers — “Murder in the City”
body: Theo is asleep on top of his comforter in his clothes for the second time today. On his MacBook a clip from tonight’s Emmys plays over and over with the sound off — Neil Patrick Harris in a tux, arms wide, mouthing a joke the room can’t hear.

Jack sits at the desk with Hale’s Williams open under the lamp. Beside one of Hale’s pencilled *No.*s he has made his first mark in the book, in pencil, a quarter inch below it: *No.* Now the page disagrees with Bernard Williams twice. Danny’s letter goes inside the Hopkins, which comes off the desk and goes into the milk crate under the bed to wait for October. Then a sheet of lined paper.

body.title: Lined paper, Delgado 412
body.text:
D —
Gina said your name to the girl. The girl looked away first. Gina wants that on the record.
The veil girl says you’re welcome.
Gina knows her name now. Lena. Don’t tell Nonna. She likes ‘the nun.’
Ohio State 38–0. Dad yelled at the TV in a good way. (Ma’s words.)
The Pacific smells like salt and kelp and money. Tell Reggie.
I’ll send the Hopkins. Ma’s right, it’s poems. Read it anyway.
—the Professor

body: He leaves Danny’s own line out of it; it’s Danny’s. Nonna he leaves for Ma to tell, on a Sunday, across a table, in the room with the vending machines.

He addresses the envelope in block capitals from memory — the name, the number, the institution, the town — and presses hard enough that the letters stand up on the back. The RAZR lies open on the desk beside it with the screen dark. There’s nothing from her tonight, and the phone can stay dark.

He folds the letter in three, along the lines, and runs his thumbnail down each crease. Across the room the clip starts over, arms wide, silent, and Theo breathes in, slow, and out, slow, and keeps on doing it.
